name: NAD+ injections

lead: NAD+ is a coenzyme every cell uses for metabolism. Some clinics sell injections or infusions of it for anti-aging, energy and recovery, and people use it hoping for fresher skin and a more youthful look.

NAD+ carries electrons in metabolic reactions and is used by sirtuin, PARP and CD38 enzymes. Proponents say injecting it raises levels that fall with age; reference sources note that human evidence for that decline is inconsistent. Registered human trials of injectable NAD+ address specific medical conditions such as hematopoietic recovery, hearing loss and vascular aging.

paras: It is given at wellness and longevity clinics as an injection or an IV infusion, often as part of a broader anti-aging or energy package. Users describe it as a periodic treatment and report effects on energy and how they feel.

Experts quoted in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown. It is not licensed as a medicine in the UK. Clinic marketing claims for aging and appearance have not been tested in controlled human trials.

social.title: How peptide injections became the answer to everything

angle.text: Longevity clinics and online communities promote injected NAD+ to raise cellular NAD+ levels, with the aim of better cellular energy and repair and fresher, more youthful-looking skin. The appearance claim rests on cell biology and user reports; registered human trials address other conditions.

lead: NAD+ injections are injected or intravenously infused preparations of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a coenzyme present in every living cell. Wellness, longevity and some aesthetic clinics offer them, and they are discussed online, for energy, recovery, mental clarity and an anti-aging effect that people hope will show in the skin, the eyes and general vitality.[1][2]

The route from an NAD+ drip to a better-looking face is a claimed, chained one: proponents say that NAD+ levels fall with age, that replacing it supports cellular repair and energy metabolism, and that healthier cells translate into healthier-looking skin, better sleep and more energy for training. NAD+ itself is thoroughly characterised biochemistry; whether injected NAD+ produces visible changes in appearance has not been tested in a controlled human trial that the wiki could locate.[1][3]

Research on NAD+ metabolism is large and active. It covers sirtuins, DNA-repair enzymes and mitochondrial function, and a growing set of human trials of oral precursors such as nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide mononucleotide. Registered trials of injectable NAD+ (called coenzyme I for injection in many Chinese registrations) concern specific medical conditions rather than appearance.[4][5][6][7][8]
In the United Kingdom NAD+ is not licensed as a medicine, and experts quoted in reference works say that the efficacy and long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ are unknown.[1]

paras: NAD+ is a coenzyme that shuttles electrons in redox reactions of metabolism, including the pathways that turn food into cellular energy. It is also consumed as a substrate by signalling enzymes: the sirtuins, the PARP family involved in DNA repair, and the CD38 enzyme.[1][3][9]

Cells make NAD+ mainly through a salvage pathway in which the enzyme NAMPT produces nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is converted to NAD+. Dietary vitamin B3 forms, namely nicotinic acid, nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside, feed these pathways.[1][4]

Arthur Harden and William John Young reported a heat-stable yeast 'coferment' that accelerated fermentation in 1906. Hans von Euler-Chelpin identified it as a nucleotide sugar phosphate in the 1930s, and Otto Warburg showed its role in hydride transfer in 1936.[1]

Conrad Elvehjem linked nicotinamide to the cure of 'black tongue' in 1938 and 1939, and Jack Preiss and Philip Handler described the biosynthetic intermediates in 1958. Shin-ichiro Imai and colleagues, working in Leonard Guarente's laboratory, discovered the NAD+-dependent sirtuins in 2000, and Charles Brenner's group described the nicotinamide riboside kinase route to NAD+ in 2004.[1]

Imai proposed an 'NAD World' hypothesis in 2009, linking sirtuin 1 and NAMPT to aging and longevity, and revised it as 'NAD World 2.0' in 2016.[1] These ideas are the intellectual basis for the anti-aging marketing around NAD+.

Researchers have proposed that a decline in cellular NAD+ during aging contributes to age-related disease, for example through reduced sirtuin activity and weaker DNA repair as PARP and CD38 consume more of the pool.[3][9] One reported mechanism is that increased binding of DBC1 to PARP1 as NAD+ falls may impair DNA repair.[1]

Human evidence on the decline is described as inconsistent and tissue dependent. A 2026 cross-sectional study of 1,068 adults, summarised in the encyclopedia record, found whole-blood NAD+ stable in men, slightly higher in women, and lower in people with cardiovascular disease, though it cannot show causation. A widely cited 2024 rat study reporting an age-related decline was withdrawn after image manipulation was found.[1]

sections.h: Use in clinics and online communities
paras: Clinics typically present NAD+ drips as a recovery and longevity service alongside vitamin infusions. The format descends from the 'Myers' cocktail' of the 1960s and the later boutique IV clinics, the first of which Wikipedia dates to Tokyo in 2008.[2]

In the UK, high-cost NAD+ infusions have also been marketed for alcohol and drug dependence, claims that medical experts quoted in reference works describe as untested.[1] The reference record notes that such marketing likely breaches advertising and medicines rules.[1]

On looksmax.org, NAD+ appears mainly in the wider conversation about injectables, peptides and anabolic or growth-related compounds, where users ask about somatropin, local IGF-1, glutathione for skin tone and similar products.[10][11][12] The community talk of NAD+ is largely about energy, sleep and a general 'glow', and is thin compared with discussion of peptides and hormones. A broader peptide boom has been covered in technology and health media.[13]

subs.h: Oral precursors as an alternative route
paras: Many people who want to raise NAD+ use oral precursors instead of injections. Nicotinamide riboside was designated a new dietary ingredient by the US FDA in 2015 and 2017 and accepted as generally recognised as safe in 2016, and the EU authorised it for supplements in 2020.[4] ChromaDex, renamed Niagen Bioscience in 2025, brands it Niagen; Elysium Health and ChromaDex were in a patent dispute from 2016 to 2023.[4]

NMN faced a 2022 FDA position that blocked its sale as a supplement because it was under investigation as a drug; the encyclopedia record says that position was later rescinded for the beta form, citing news and an FDA letter from late 2025.[5]

No controlled trials of injected NAD+ for skin, appearance or healthy-aging outcomes were found. A registered trial (NCT06919328), recruiting since 2024 with 70 participants, compares absorption and tolerability of an injectable nicotinamide riboside product with NAD+ in healthy aging; no results were located.[7]

Other registered injectable-NAD+ trials concern hematopoietic recovery after cord blood transplantation (phase 1, 12 participants), sudden sensorineural hearing loss (36 participants), immune thrombocytopenia, vascular aging (60 participants) and, planned for 2026, pediatric cardiac dysfunction (180 participants). They are small, mostly early-phase and not appearance studies.[8][14][15][16][17]

Human trials of oral precursors are better developed. A 10-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese found that NMN raised muscle insulin sensitivity.[6] A 60-day randomized multicenter trial in 80 healthy middle-aged adults tested oral NMN at several doses for efficacy and safety.[18]

The NADPARK phase I trial tested nicotinamide riboside in Parkinson's disease, a randomized trial examined it in older adults with mild cognitive impairment, and another randomized trial examined long-term safety and metabolism of NIAGEN in healthy overweight adults.[19][20][21] These studies concern oral supplements and medical or metabolic outcomes, not injectable NAD+ or looks.
A 2025 mouse study reported that NAD+ attenuated demyelination in an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis model.[22]

Experts quoted in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown, and no safety data from controlled trials of cosmetic or longevity use were found.[1] General risks of intravenous therapy include infection, sepsis, phlebitis and infiltration, and the encyclopedia record notes that technique and oversight at storefront clinics can affect the risk.[2]

NAD+ is not approved or licensed as a medicine in the UK.[1] Reports of injected products in other cosmetic fields give a sense of the monitoring that exists for approved injectables: a systematic review of cosmetic botulinum toxin injections catalogued their complications and noted limited regulation of the field.[23]
The WADA rule limiting intravenous infusions to 100 mL per 12 hours without an exemption is relevant to athletes who use IV services.[2]
Related offerings include vitamin and glutathione infusions, oral NMN or NR supplements, peptide injections, and niacin or nicotinamide products for skin. Each is discussed separately on the wiki.
